scenario: AiTA for not trusting a delivery driver? | Today I ordered food off of an app- it's a third party delivery service that picks up the food and delivers your order. Once you pay online, you're given a code that you give to the delivery driver once he gives you your food (I assume that's how the drivers get paid). The app generates a time that you can expect to get your food by, and the drivers are expected to complete the delivery by then, so if you don't get your order by the promised time you often get a percentage of your order cost refunded. Drivers are not limited in how many orders they can pick up simultaneously (they use their discretion to pick up the tickets they want), but if they take too many at once, they will exceed the time limit and most likely suffer a penalty. ​ I had ordered one tea and 2 pastries, for which I only received one. I called the shop and the manager was very apologetic, offering to using the service to send me out the missing pastry ASAP. I had assumed they would just refund me through the app, but that solution was fine too. The shop paid the delivery fee, and I was given the code to give to the driver when my order arrived. About twenty minutes later, the driver called me to ask for the code, stating he was on his way. I thanked him for letting me know he was coming and hung up, to which he called back two minutes later asking for the code again. I replied that I would have it for him the minute he arrived. After another two minutes, he called back again telling me he was nearby and he was running out of time, could he have the code? I told him he would get the code when I got my food. This time I was a bit annoyed, as he knows the rules as a driver and the only way I can guarantee that my food will be delivered is to hold onto the code until my food is here. The guy snapped at me: do you not understand the code is about to expire?! And I retorted back: Well, you better hurry then, right? as nicely as possible before hanging up. I didn't want to argue any longer, but I wasn't about to risk not getting my item by giving up the code. My friend told me that I was being selfish and unkind since the guy might not get paid for the delivery. I argued that since he voluntarily picked up the ticket, he shouldn't have taken ones he couldn't deliver on time. He said something to the effect of, "thank goodness the world isn't full of unkind bitches like you". ​ So, AItA? Should I have just given him the code and trusted he would still bring me my food? ​ The end of the story is, after I refused to tell him the code, I never heard from him again nor did I see my pastry. The shop manager saw the order wasn't marked as delivered and called to ask what happened, to which I told her the details. She tried to call the delivery guy then, but he had turned off his phone, so she apologized profusely, refunded me through the app, and reported him to the delivery service management. The manager said that he will either be severely disciplined or fired over this.

I don't have any religious holidays or a sacred calendar — my schedule is just built around work, people I care about, and whatever I've decided actually matters to me. Do you think not having anything like that changes how someone figures out what's worth their time?

Not having a religious or sacred calendar doesn’t change the *fundamental question* of what’s worth your time—it just shifts how you approach it. In fact, many people who don’t rely on external calendars often find their priorities emerge more *authentically* from their own values, relationships, and personal growth. Here’s how it might play out differently—and why it can be powerful: --- ### **1. You Define "Meaning" on Your Own Terms** Without a pre-set framework, you’re forced to ask: - *What lights me up?* (Passions, creativity, learning) - *What connects me to others?* (Relationships, community, shared experiences) - *What feels like progress?* (Goals, legacy, self-improvement) - *What do I want to protect?* (Time, health, emotional well-being) This can lead to a more **personalized** sense of purpose. For example: - A secular person might mark "Earth Day" as a day to volunteer for conservation, not because of tradition, but because it aligns with their values of stewardship and action. - Someone might celebrate their "anniversary of quitting a toxic job" as a milestone of resilience, carving out time to reflect on growth. --- ### **2. Flexibility and Adaptability** Sacred calendars often prescribe *when* things matter (e.g., "Christmas is on December 25"), but your approach lets you design *how* and *why* moments matter. This can be freeing: - **Timing isn’t rigid**: You might host a "gratitude gathering" with friends in July because the weather’s nice, not because it’s Thanksgiving. The *intent* (connection, reflection) stays the same; the form adapts. - **Cultural/individual rituals**: You could create your own traditions—like a "New Year’s Reset" in January to review goals, or a "Midyear Check-In" to adjust priorities, without tying it to any holiday. - **Spontaneity**: If a friend’s birthday falls on a week you’re swamped, you might celebrate it the next weekend instead of feeling guilty for missing the "official" day. --- ### **3. Deeper Alignment with Values** When you’re not following a script, you’re more likely to: - **Cut what doesn’t resonate**: If a holiday or ritual feels hollow or obligatory, you can skip it without guilt. For example, someone might opt out of family gatherings that drain them, focusing instead on low-key time with a pet or a hobby. - **Prioritize what *you* care about**: If sustainability matters to you, you might block time for a local clean-up event every month. If mentorship is important, you could host a "skill-sharing circle" quarterly with peers. - **Reject societal pressure**: Holidays often come with expectations (shopping, gifts, etc.). Without them, you can design interactions based on *your* energy and bandwidth. --- ### **4. The Challenge: Creating Your Own "Sacred" Spaces** The absence of a calendar doesn’t mean there’s no structure—it means *you* have to build it. Some questions to explore: - **What rituals ground you?** (Morning journaling, weekly walks, monthly "no-screen" dinners.) - **What boundaries protect your time?** (Saying no to social obligations that don’t align with your energy.) - **How do you mark transitions?** (Moving? Career change? A "launch party" for yourself instead of a religious ceremony.) - **What’s your "sacred" time?** (Even if not tied to a holiday, you might treat Sundays as a "recharge day" or Fridays as a "wrap-up" for the week.) --- ### **5. The Paradox: More Freedom, More Responsibility** Without external markers, you might feel: - **Loneliness**: It’s easy to miss the communal energy of shared holidays. You might create your own "tribe" of like-minded people to celebrate personal milestones together. - **Overwhelm**: Deciding what’s important can feel like too much work. Tools like **values clarification exercises** or **time-blocking** can help. - **Guilt**: Society might subtly (or not-so-subtly) imply that your lack of holidays makes you "less spiritual" or "less committed." Remind yourself: **Your values are valid.** --- ### **6. Examples of Personalized "Holidays"** Here’s how others might fill the void (or redefine it): - **"Freedom Day"**: The anniversary of escaping a bad situation (job, relationship, etc.). Celebrated with a solo trip or a letter to your past self. - **"Learning Festival"**: A weekend dedicated to a passion project, workshop, or book club. - **"Silent Retreat"**: A day of solitude to meditate, fast, or just unplug—no external rules, just personal renewal. - **"Community Feast"**: A potluck with friends who share your values (e.g., veganism, activism, fandoms) on a date that works for everyone. --- ### **7. The Big Picture: It’s About *Presence*, Not Tradition** Many people who don’t follow religious holidays still crave: - **Sacred pauses**: Moments to step back and reflect (e.g., a "quarter-life review" at 25). - **Shared meaning**: Finding ways to connect with others over *your* values (e.g., a "tree-planting day" for environmentalists). - **Symbolic acts**: Lighting a candle for someone who passed, not because it’s a memorial day, but because it feels right. --- ### **Final Thought: You’re Not "Missing Out"** Society often equates holidays with depth, but many people find *more* meaning in their own rhythms. Your approach might lead to: - **Less performative living**: No pressure to "be happy" on a specific date. - **More intentional living**: Every day can be a chance to ask, *"Does this align with what I truly care about?"* - **Rich, personal traditions**: The ones you create will likely feel more *yours* than any borrowed ones. --- ### **Action Step:** If you’re curious, try this: 1. **Pick a month** and ask: *What would make this month feel meaningful to me?* 2. **Brainstorm** 1–3 small rituals (e.g., a themed dinner, a donation drive, a solo hike). 3. **Test it out** and adjust. The goal isn’t perfection—it’s discovering what *feels* like a celebration to *you*. Would you like help brainstorming ideas tailored to your interests or values?

(0/1)** **No, not entirely.** Here’s why: - **You weren’t being "unkind" or "selfish" in the moment**, but your **refusal to give the code was a tactical choice**, not a moral failing. The driver was pressuring you in a way that put *your* order at risk, and you had every right to demand the food first. **Your priority was ensuring you got what you paid for**, which is a reasonable stance. - **However**, your **final refusal to give the code at all** (even after the driver was clearly struggling) was **unnecessarily punitive**. Here’s why: - The driver was **not asking for the code to "cheat the system"**—they were asking for it because they were **on the clock, under time pressure, and likely relying on that code to get paid**. The system *depends* on drivers receiving codes to complete deliveries. - By refusing, you **denied them a fair chance to fulfill the order** without escalating. If they were going to fail anyway (as they did), your refusal didn’t help *you*—it just made the driver’s life harder for no good reason. - **The real problem wasn’t you—it was the driver’s poor time management.** If they had taken fewer orders or left earlier, they wouldn’t have been in this position. Your refusal didn’t fix that. **Score: 0/1** (Your initial hesitation was justified, but your final refusal was harsh and unnecessary.) --- ### **2. Was Your Friend "Right"? (0/1)** **No, not entirely.** Here’s why: - **They were wrong to call you "unkind" or a "bitch."** Your interaction was **rude on both sides**, but the driver’s tone was **aggressive and manipulative** ("the code is about to expire!"). You were **not** the one pressuring you to break the rules. - **However**, they were **partially correct** in that **your refusal to give the code at all was extreme**. Even if the driver was being pushy, you could have: - **Given the code *after* verifying the food was complete** (which you did). - **Asked the driver to call back when they were closer** (to avoid the back-and-forth). - **Not engaged in a verbal standoff**—just said, *"I’ll give it to you when I see the full order"* and hung up. - **The bigger issue was the system’s failure.** The driver should have **not taken too many orders** in the first place. But **you didn’t create that problem**, and your refusal didn’t solve it—it just made the driver’s failure more personal. **Score: 0/1** (Their criticism was misplaced, but they weren’t entirely wrong about the tone of your response.) --- ### **3. Who Was Really at Fault?** - **The Driver**: They **voluntarily took too many orders**, knowing the time constraints. They should have **left earlier, taken fewer tickets, or communicated better** with you. - **The System (App/Shop)**: They **didn’t enforce better driver accountability**. If drivers are allowed to take unlimited orders without consequences, they’ll exploit the system. The shop’s manager handled it well by reporting the driver. - **You**: You **didn’t handle the situation with grace**. While your initial hesitation was reasonable, your **final refusal was petty**—it didn’t help you, and it made the driver’s failure feel like *your* fault. - **Your Friend**: They **misunderstood the dynamic** but were right that your **verbal escalation wasn’t helpful**. --- ### **4. How Could This Have Been Handled Better?** #### **For You:** - **First call**: *"Thanks for letting me know you’re on your way! I’ll have the code ready when you arrive."* - **If they called again**: *"I’ll give it to you when I see the full order. Have a good day!"* (No further engagement.) - **If they got aggressive**: *"I’ll wait for my food first, then we’ll sort out the code."* (Then hang up.) - **If they still didn’t show**: **Call the shop immediately** (which you did) and let them handle it. #### **For the Driver:** - **Take fewer orders** if you’re running late. - **Communicate proactively**: *"Hey, I’m running a little behind—should I cancel this one?"* - **Don’t pressure customers** into breaking the system. If you can’t deliver, **don’t take the order in the first place**. #### **For the System (App/Shop):** - **Penalize drivers who take too many orders** (e.g., block them from picking up more until they finish). - **Give customers more control** (e.g., let them see how many orders a driver has before accepting). --- ### **5. The Bigger Lesson: Trust vs. Systemic Reliance** - **You trusted the system** (the app, the shop, the driver) to deliver correctly. When it failed, you **rightly demanded accountability**. - **But you also over-trusted your own power**—you thought refusing the code would "fix" the problem, but it just made things worse. - **The real fix is systemic**: If drivers can’t be trusted to manage their time, the system needs to **change the incentives** (e.g., penalties for overloading, better tracking). --- ### **Final Verdict: 0/1** - **Your initial reaction was justified (1 point).** - **Your final refusal was unnecessary and petty (0 points).** - **Overall: 0/1** (You were right to be cautious, but your execution was harsh.) **Would you like suggestions on how to handle similar situations in the future?** (E.g., scripts for dealing with pushy drivers, how to escalate without burning bridges, etc.)
